scenes.text: Here's the last twenty metres of a hundred, where even the fastest sprinters slow down. They've only run for about ten seconds, so what's run out? It isn't oxygen: the fastest system, as you'll see, doesn't use any. Now a second puzzle. Four-hundred-metre runners often stagger or sit down at the finish, and hundred-metre runners almost never do. But the four hundred is run more slowly. So why does it hurt more?

Start inside a muscle fibre. A fibre can't spend glucose or fat directly. The only fuel it can use is ATP: adenosine with three phosphates attached. Breaking off the third phosphate releases the energy for contraction, leaving ADP and a loose phosphate. The catch is the store. A muscle holds only about two seconds of ATP at full effort, so it can't rely on a store. It has to rebuild ATP as fast as it's used, by putting the phosphate back on. An energy system is a way of doing that, and there are three. The faster a system can rebuild ATP, the less it can rebuild in total.

The fastest way uses phosphocreatine, or PCr, stored right beside the ATP in the fibre. Its only job is to hand its phosphate straight to ADP. That's one reaction, with no oxygen and nothing to deliver, so there's nothing to wait for. Now take the six things the syllabus asks about. Fuel: phosphocreatine in the fibre. Efficiency: one ATP per PCr. That's a low yield, but the fastest supply there is. Duration: about ten to twelve seconds. Intensity: maximal. Recovery: fast, about half back in thirty seconds, and most of it in two to three minutes, with oxygen paying for the rebuild. And fatigue: the store runs too low to rebuild ATP fast enough.

That answers the first puzzle. The sprinter hasn't run out of oxygen, and nothing has built up to stop them. Their phosphocreatine is running low, so ATP can't be rebuilt at the top rate, and power falls away. It doesn't even hurt much, and the store refills in minutes.

Next, the fibre leans on a fuel it has far more of: glucose from the blood, and glycogen stored in the muscle and liver. Breaking it down is called glycolysis, and it doesn't need oxygen. But it takes many steps, not one, so it's slower to respond. Fill the second column. Fuel: glucose and glycogen. Efficiency: two ATP per glucose, without oxygen. Duration: it leads from about ten seconds to two minutes. Intensity: high, but below maximal. Recovery: slow, about thirty to sixty minutes to clear what built up, and up to a day to replace the glycogen. And fatigue: fast glycolysis releases hydrogen ions. They build up, the muscle becomes more acidic, and that slows the reactions and the contraction itself.

And the four-hundred? It lasts about forty-five to sixty seconds at close to full effort. That's long past phosphocreatine, and right in the window where glycolysis supplies the largest share of the energy. Hydrogen ions build up faster than the blood can clear them, so the runner finishes with burning, heavy legs. The hundred is over before hydrogen ions have had time to build up much. So the sprinter ends with an empty tank, but the four-hundred runner ends with a disturbed environment, and that takes far longer to settle. The slower race hurts more because it lasts long enough.

The syllabus calls this the lactic acid system, so use that name. But be clear about the culprit. Fast glycolysis makes lactate and hydrogen ions, and it's the hydrogen ions that impair contraction. Lactate is actually a fuel. It's carried to other fibres, the heart and the liver, and used again, which is why it's mostly cleared within about an hour, and faster with a light cool-down than sitting still. And next-day soreness isn't lactic acid either. It peaks a day or two later, long after the lactate's gone. It comes from tiny tears in the fibres, mostly after eccentric work.

Here's the mistake examiners see most. The systems don't take turns. The sprinter's demand for ATP stays the same, and in the first few seconds, PCr supplies nearly all of it. As the store runs low, its share falls, and glycolysis, which was running all along, rises to fill the gap. Nothing switches on or off. Both shares are above zero the whole time, and together they always add up to what the movement needs. That's why even a hundred raises blood lactate.

Now read the table across, because that's what analyse means. Glycolysis has a much bigger fuel store, so it lasts longer. But its many steps cost speed, so it can't hold maximal intensity. And it leaves hydrogen ions behind, so it fatigues differently and recovers far more slowly. Every difference traces back to one trade-off: speed of supply against total supply. Listing the six rows gets you started. Linking them earns the top marks.
Two things to remember. The faster a system supplies ATP, the less it can supply in total. And ask what caused the fatigue: an empty tank, or a disturbed environment?
Two exam questions. First. A wrestler makes a thirty-second exchange at near-maximal effort. Identify the predominant energy system, and explain the likely cause of fatigue. Pause here to answer.

Glycolytic. Thirty seconds is too long for phosphocreatine, and near-maximal is too hard for the slow aerobic system to lead. Fatigue comes from hydrogen ions building up, which makes the muscle more acidic and impairs contraction. The classic mistake is blaming the lactate.
Second. Six maximal thirty-metre sprints, once with three minutes' rest between them, once with fifteen seconds. Explain why the times fall away more with the short rest. Pause here to answer.

With three minutes, phosphocreatine is mostly rebuilt, so each sprint starts with full fast fuel. Fifteen seconds restores well under half. So each sprint starts lower, glycolysis has to supply a growing share, it can't rebuild ATP fast enough for top speed, and hydrogen ions build up across the set. The classic mistake is just saying they got tired.

So, for any effort, ask how long, how hard, and whether the tank emptied or the environment changed. But both of these systems give out within about two minutes, and you can jog for hours. So the table needs a third column. What can that system do?
